title: Project 1: Small Molecule Entry Inhibitors of Pandemic Viruses
text:
Project 1 – Small Molecule Entry Inhibitors of Pandemic Viruses
NARRATIVE
 Receptor binding and refolding of the fusion protein, followed by lipid mixing, are three essential entry
steps to release the genome of enveloped viruses to initiate replication. Inhibitors of any one of the three steps
may be developed as effective antiviral drugs. We have devised strategies to design small molecule entry
inhibitors of coronaviruses (CoVs), arenaviruses (Arv), flaviviruses (FLAVs) and filoviruses (FiVs).

title: Cell-free DNA Analysis for Liquid Biopsy of Cancer
text:
The proposed research in the first phase of this proposal is to investigate a new methodology to capture and
define a novel ultrashort circulating tumor DNA species in the plasma of lung cancer patients. In the second
phase, the usage of various other molecules additional to the ultrashort DNA species in biofluids will be explored
in hopes to detect multiple cancer types with liquid biopsy. These findings will contribute to improved clinical
outcomes for cancer patients by leading to the development of new liquid biopsy approaches for improved
detection and treatment monitoring.

title: Mass Spectrometry/Proteomics Core
text: VDDRC MASS SPECTROMETRY (MS) AND PROTEOMICS CORE The MS/Proteomics Core provides cost-effective, state-of-the-art instrumentation and expertise to investigators in the Vanderbilt Digestive Disease Research Center (VDDRC). This core leverages the expert personnel and cutting edge instrument facilities located in the Vanderbilt Mass Spectrometry Research Center to provide specialized services to VDDRC members. This core will be used for identification and quantification of small molecules, identification, characterization, and quantification of proteins, and biomolecular tissue imaging and profiling. Fifty-eight VDDRC investigators have used the core extensively during the current funding period for digestive disease-related projects leading to 73 peer-reviewed original publications. Services used include: analytical method development, assistance with experimental design, inductively coupled MS, multiplex quantitative proteomics with isotope tagging methods, phosphoproteome characterization, identification of post-translational modifications, elemental analysis by ICP-MS, molecular profiling, tissue imaging, and bioinformatics analysis. Core personnel perform assays for investigators and provided a formalized training program to 45 trainees from VDDRC Member laboratories on the theoretical and practical aspects of MS during the current funding period. The small molecule/metabolite component of the Core is run as an open-access facility in which users can choose to prepare their samples and operate the instruments. Proteomics samples are submitted to the core for analysis by proteomics staff after consultations between the investigator and core staff on the most appropriate experimental design, sample preparation and instrumental analysis methods. Administrative staff monitor the use of the instrument facilities by investigators and prepare reports on utilization for use by the Administrative Core. The core has 25 mass spectrometers available to users, in addition to specialized instrumentation for advanced analyses. The Specific Aims of the Core are to: 1) Provide access to state-of-the-art mass spectrometry equipment for analysis of small molecule drugs and endogenous metabolites (host and microbial), including focused and discovery metabolomics, in an open-access analytical facility; 2) Provide access to a state-of-the-art proteomics facility for identification, characterization, and quantitation of proteins and whole proteomes in digestive disease-related samples; 3) Provide access to a pioneering imaging mass spectrometry facility for spatial localization of proteins, peptides, lipids, metabolites, and drugs in GI tissues; 4) Provide professional guidance on experimental design, development of analytical assays, and data interpretation; 5) Train users on digestive diseases sample preparation, instrument operation, and data analysis; 6) Train users on bioinformatics analysis of complex proteomic data; 7) Promote interactions between other VDDRC Cores to facilitate and enhance the collaborative mission of the VDDRC research enterprise.

title: Gene delivery to antigen-specific T cells via targeted retroviral vectors to treat cancer
text:
Viral gene delivery strategies that could expand and transduce tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in vivo, without the
need for ex vivo manipulations would be highly desirable. Here we optimize and streamline a peptide-MHC viral
platform for in vivo gene delivery to tumor-specific T cells, bypassing ex vivo culture steps and avoiding off-target
T cells. This approach could be used for any antigen specificity and any therapeutic cargo.

title: An exploratory study of a new pH-responsive, ionizable hybrid nanocarrier for enchancing drug accumulation in bacterial biofilms
text:
In this project, we will develop a new nanocarrier (small devices about the size of one millionth of a millimeter)
that can carry combination of antiretrovirals to the bacterial biofilms (aggregates of bacteria grown on patients'
tissues or medical devices) in a specific and efficient manner. The proposed nanocarrier is designed to respond
to the acidity in the biofilms and turn from neutral to positively charged, so it will accumulate within the
negatively charged biofilms by electrostatic attraction to achieve high drug levels there. Successful completion
of this project will have a major impact in advancing the treatment of various biofilm-associated infections
which often respond poorly to the current antimicrobial therapy.

title: Mechanism of Toxin Mediated Damage to the Lung Epithelium during S. pneumoniae Infection
text:
Streptococcus pneumoniae causes over 150,000 hospitalizations annually in the U.S., with a
mortality rate of 5-7%, making the disease both a significant health and financial burden. The goal
of the proposed research is to elucidate the role of a S. pneumoniae toxin in damaging the lung
epithelium, a crucial event that promotes bacterial dissemination from the lungs to the blood and
causes more severe disease. Understanding how this toxin contributes to more severe outcomes
in patients will help us design novel therapies to combat pneumoniae and other lung infections.

title: SCH: Toward a smart, home-use system for noninvasive, personalized monitoring of drug levels
text:
RELEVANCE (See instructions):
Optimizing the dose of epilepsy medication to suppress seizures and minimize side effects can be an
ongoing struggle. Although knowing the drug's level in the body would be expected to help guide dosing,
laboratory measurement of drug levels in blood is inconvenient and slow. We propose to create and
validate a device that could be used by a patient to measure (using chemical sensing and Al) the drug
level in their saliva in order to rapidly find their optimal dosing plan and improve their quality of life.

title: Characterization of potent antivirals targeting HBV capsid
text:
Despite the availability of vaccines, Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) continues to be a global health and economic burden,
as nearly 300 million people worldwide are infected and there is currently no cure. Antiviral compounds that
target the HBV capsid are being studied as potential new therapies for HBV treatment. This proposal will use
cutting-edge techniques to provide the first information on how a new class of capsid-targeting antivirals affect
HBV capsid assembly and aggregation, toward the development of novel therapeutic strategies to eradicate and
cure HBV.

title: Software for rapid assessment of human movement dynamics using a handheld smartphone
text:
Interventions to slow age-related mobility impairment can be effective, but they are often prescribed after
significant functional decline has already occurred—earlier detection is needed. Changes in movement
biomechanics could likely predict the onset of conditions like osteoarthritis and frailty, but little is known about
this process because incorporating lab-based biomechanical measures in large prospective studies is costly
and time intensive. To address this, we aim to develop software that quantifies human movement
biomechanics in minutes using a single handheld smartphone, enabling the prospective studies needed to
uncover the biomechanical predictors of mobility decline and, ultimately, providing a tool for low-cost risk
screening.

title: Application of a mobile health platform for assessing cognition and psychiatric symptoms in Veterans
text:
Technology holds the potential to aid in understanding the real-world phenomenology of risk for suicide,
including identifying potential targets for early intervention. This project will employ smartphone-delivered tests
of specific cognitive variables and examine real-time relationships between cognitive dysfunction, negative
emotions and social contexts, and suicide risk in Veterans. This pilot project implements mobile health tools for
understanding the cognitive mechanisms underlying suicidal ideation outside of the laboratory, setting the
stage for future mechanistic and intervention research.

title: Targeting branched-chain keto acid accumulation in melanoma leptomeningeal disease
text:
Leptomeningeal disease (LMD) is a devastating condition for late-stage melanoma patients when their tumors
spread to the membranes lining the brain and spinal cord, characterized by poor outcomes, severe neurologic
symptoms, and resistance to most therapies. In this proposal, we will 1) find out if certain substances called
branched-chain keto acids (BCKA) support tumor growth, metabolism, and survival at this unique metastatic site,
2) identify how BCKA inhibit anti-tumor immune activity and 3) determine the best therapy to lower BCKA levels
as a strategy to treat LMD. These studies will establish how BCKA contribute to the aggressive nature of LMD
and provide a preclinical rationale for adopting BCKA-lowering therapies for the treatment of LMD.

title: Microbiome Core: IDEAL shapes vaccine response, susceptibility to respiratory infectious disease and asthma
text: Microbiome Core, Summary Mounting evidence indicates a strong association between the microbiome and immune development in early life (IDEAL). More specifically, we and others are providing growing evidence for a role of the microbiome in the three clinical outcomes targeted in this IDEAL proposal: vaccine response, respiratory infection, and asthma. In support of the proposed IDEAL program, the Microbiome Core (MBC) will generate and analyze shotgun metagenomes from 1300 nasal and fecal samples from the existing Rochester Combined Cohort (RCC) and the prospective Rochester IDEAL Cohort (RIC). Data generation and analyses will be conducted with rigorous quality assurance measures. The microbiome data, paired with clinical and other omic data, will be exceptional for an IDEAL study, and the nasal metagenomes will be unprecedented in scope and depth of microbiome coverage. The premise at the foundation of the MBC is that the microbiome is a key driver of IDEAL. As a consequence, we hypothesize that the microbiome will contribute to key objectives of the overall IDEAL proposal, (i) early prediction of clinical phenotypes, (ii) delineation of molecular endotypes among the phenotypes, and (iii) identification of actionable therapeutic targets. Further, comparative analysis of microbiomes will provide mechanistic insight to interactions between the microbiome and IDEAL. The MBC has two Specific Aims: SA1 is to generate microbiome data products, (i) high-quality shotgun metagenome sequence data, (ii) taxonomic profiles, and (iii) functional profiles. The data products will be transferred to the Data Management Core (DMC) to support Projects (PR) 1-3 in addressing the above key objectives. SA2 is microbiome analysis using both taxonomic and functional profiles, focussing on diversity, differential abundance, temporal dynamics, and interactions. The main purpose of the MBC analyses will be ecological and mechanistic interpretation of microbiome variability among the clinical phenotypes and molecular endotypes.

title: A Human iPSC-derived Microphysiological 3D model to study CAA/AD
text:
Most Alzheimer’s disease patients have an associated vascular brain disease, Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy, in
which abnormal amyloid protein builds up around blood vessels. This weakens the blood-brain-barrier, resulting
in microbleeds and hemorrhages, causing further brain damage. We aim to build a state-of-the-art 3D human
stem cell-derived model with open blood vessels that will allow us to study how genetic risk factors such as
APOE4 and environmental factors in the brain and blood cause vascular pathology and how they may be
reversed.

title: Targeting PP4 to improve ovarian cancer response to immunotherapy
text:
The immune response is highly active in ovarian cancer, but ovarian tumors do not respond well to immune
checkpoint blockade (ICB). We propose to investigate whether inhibition of DNA damage repair by blocking the
function of the protein phosphatase 4 complex during chemotherapy will increase immunogenicity in ovarian
cancer and enhance response to ICB. Ultimately, such knowledge has the potential to inform the development
of new therapies benefiting many types of cancer.

title: Immunology Research Training Grant
text:
There is continued need to train young researchers who will apply cutting-edge knowledge and
interdisciplinary techniques to increase our understanding of the role of immunology and
inflammation in infectious diseases, in cancer immunotherapy, and in chronic degenerative
diseases such as Alzheimer’s Disease and muscular dystrophies. Following the COVID-19
pandemic, there is also an urgent need to understand protective immunity and the role of the
immune system in mediating tissue damage to the lungs and disease severity. A T32 training
grant will enable us to continue to provide opportunities for predoctoral students to develop
expertise in multiple aspects of the immune response and support our ongoing very successful
Immunology Training Program.

title: CRCNS: Open Data Commons for Stroke Research - Promoting FAIR Data Through Community-Driven Design
text:
RELEVANCE (See instructions):
ODC-Stroke, a FAIR data platform, will enable researchers to securely share, integrate, and analyze
preclinical stroke data at scale thereby improving health research. By supporting reproducible science,
advanced Al-driven analyses, and cross-study comparisons, the platform will accelerate the discovery
and translation of more effective stroke therapies, ultimately leading to improved outcomes for patients
affected by stroke and related neurological disorders directly supporting the mission of NINDS.

title: Glomerular endothelial damage: a new role of the lipids in Alport syndrome
text:
Emerging evidence implicates previously unknown glomerular endothelial lipid dysfunction as an
important pathological process in the development of Alport syndrome. In this proposal we will
investigate the role of lipid metabolism in the development of glomerular endothelial dysfunction and
will use extracellular vesicles as a tool to re-establish functional homeostasis. Better understanding of
the role of glomerular endothelium in the development of Alport pathology will facilitate the discovery
of strategies to more effectively target the kidney for therapy.

title: Patch-based deep scRNA-Seq to understand axon repair in the mammalian spinal cord
text:
Promoting axon regeneration remains an important strategy in order to identify effective restorative treatment for
spinal cord injury. This proposal will using a cutting-edge experimental approach, Patch-seq, to better understand
the neuron intrinsic control of regenerative process. New insights gained will be valuable in designing therapies
to promote repair and recovery after spinal cord injury.

title: Molecular Mechanisms of Ribbon Synapse Formation in the Inner Ear
text:
The synapses between inner hair cells and Type I spiral ganglion neurons of the inner ear are highly specialized
and are critical for hearing. This study proposes to study the molecular mechanisms of synapse formation in the
inner ear with a focus on synaptic adhesion molecules. These studies will deepen our understanding of synapse
formation and specification in the inner ear and could promote the development of novel therapeutics to prevent
and protect against hearing loss.

title: Research Training in Biomedical Informatics and Data Science at Oregon Health & Science University
text: The Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU) National Library of Medicine (NLM) T15 Biomedical Informatics Training Program trains future researchers and leaders in biomedical and health informatics, the field devoted to improving personal health, health care, public health, and biomedical research through the use of data, information, and their associated technologies. This NLM Training Grant will enable us to support predoctoral (PhD students) and postdoctoral trainees pursuing courses, an in-depth research project, and related academic activities. This proposal is a competitive renewal for a seventh five-year cycle of funding for the OHSU program, which has been a leader and innovator in the program for three decades.
